CausalChain: Green tea catechins (e.g., EGCG) ingestion -> Catechins chelate metal ions and modulate ROS levels -> Reduced stabilization of HIF-1α and decreased immunosuppressive cytokine expression -> Shift in tumor-associated macrophage phenotype from M2 (pro-tumorigenic) to M1 (anti-tumorigenic) -> Enhanced anti-tumor immune response and increased cancer cell apoptosis
Hypothesis: Green tea catechins can reprogram tumor-associated macrophages by modulating cellular redox status and chelating pro-oxidative metal ions, thereby shifting TAMs from an immunosuppressive M2 phenotype to a tumoricidal M1 phenotype, which enhances anti-tumor immunity.
Abstract: This study proposes that green tea catechins, particularly EGCG, may possess an underexplored ability to reprogram tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs) from a pro-tumorigenic M2 phenotype to an anti-tumorigenic M1 phenotype via redox modulation and metal ion chelation. Building on existing evidence regarding the antioxidant, pro-oxidant, and metal chelating properties of catechins, we hypothesize that low to moderate doses of green tea catechins can alter the tumor microenvironment by moderating intracellular reactive oxygen species (ROS) levels. This redox shift is expected to reduce stabilization of HIF-1α and the subsequent expression of immunosuppressive cytokines, thus promoting M1 polarization. The enhanced M1 phenotype, in turn, may improve the anti-tumor immune response and synergize with conventional therapies. Future experimental approaches should investigate the molecular signaling events linking catechin-mediated redox modulation to TAM polarization and assess the subsequent impact on tumor progression.
